abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: To identify chromosomal regions and candidate genes controlling important wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) traits under heat stress, a doubled haploid population was developed from a cross between KSG0057, a selection out of PBW343 and KSG1190, a heat stress tolerant line. The population was evaluated for grain yield, 100‐grain weight, grain weight of main spike, number of grains per main spike, number of spikelets per main spike, spike length, and plant height during 2016–2017 and 2017–2018 at two locations in India. Heat stress was applied by conducting trials under normal, late, and very late sown conditions. The mapping population was genotyped using sequencing‐based genotyping to target the genic fraction of the genome. A 3875.3 cM linkage map was constructed via 674 high‐quality single nucleotide polymorphisms. Composite interval mapping was done for individual environments and for reduction percentage due to late and very late planting. With 38 regions common between the two types of analysis, 66 genomic regions containing 155 quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for individual environments and 100 containing 152 QTLs for the reduction percentage analysis were identified. Of the 155 QTLs, 82 were found only under very late sown conditions. Of the 152 QTLs, 40 were for heat stress and 45 for severe heat stress. The QTL‐containing regions ranged from 1.5 kb to 684.9 Mb in size, with 35 being <1 Mb and 30 being <5 Mb. Number of genes in these 35 regions ranged from 1 to 19. Candidate genes for 16 of the regions were identified as the underlying region of 1.5–287.5 kb contained only one gene each.

list-item.p: Three hundred seven quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for seven agronomic traits, including yield, were mapped by genotyping a DH population of 196 lines.
A total of 128 regions having 307 QTLs under normal and heat stress conditions were mapped on 21 chromosomes.
Of these, 40 were for mild heat stress and 45 for severe heat stress with one being common.
Of the 128 QTL‐containing regions, the size of 18 was <100 kb and 17 was <1 Mb.
16 of the 128 regions had only one candidate gene and 16 other regions had 2–10 candidate genes.

abstract.title: Plain Language Summary
abstract.p: To identify chromosomal regions and candidate genes controlling important traits under terminal heat stress, a doubled haploid population of 192 lines involving two parents contrasting for the trait was evaluated for seven traits under normal, mild, and severe heat stress for 2 years at two locations. The population was genotyped using sequencing‐based genotyping enriched for the genic fraction of the genome with an average of 1 million reads per line. Quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping for the normal, mild heat stress, and severe heat stress conditions identified 128 regions containing 155 QTLs for normal and 152 for the heat stress conditions. Of the 152 QTLs, 40 were for mild heat stress and 45 for severe heat stress. The size of the QTL‐containing regions ranged from 1.5 kb to 684.9 Mb, with 35 being <1 Mb having number of genes ranged from 1 to 19. Of these, 16 regions contained only one gene; thus, these candidate genes were accurately identified.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is a major cereal crop grown under temperate environmental conditions. It is a major source of nutrition providing protein and calories to a large part of the global population, which necessitates its higher production around the world. However, wheat production is challenged by several biotic and abiotic factors. Among the abiotic factors, temperature plays an important role in determining wheat productivity. Wheat, being a cool‐season crop, requires an optimum temperature of 15°C–20°C for the growth and grain development. Especially during grain development, every 1°C rise in temperature above 28°C reduces the grain yield (GY) by 3%–4% (I. Wardlaw et al., 1989). The high temperature during the grain filling stage shortens the crop duration and affects the pollen fertility, which in turn adversely affects the grain weight and grain number, the two most important traits determining wheat GY (Plaut et al., 2004; Tashiro & Wardlaw, 1990).

Yield is a complex trait governed by several component traits; therefore, optimal expression of these traits is vital to realize the full yield potential of wheat varieties under heat stress (HS) (Reynolds et al., 2009). Reduction in wheat yield due to HS may be the result of pollen sterility or grain abortion leading to reduced grain number (Tashiro & Wardlaw, 1990). HS also leads to reduced starch and protein accumulation (Bhullar & Jenner, 1985), grain weight (Stone & Nicolas, 1995), grain size (I. F. Wardlaw, 1994), biomass, increased assimilation of CO2 (Wollenweber et al., 2003), and early senescence (Vijayalakshmi et al., 2010). Therefore, genetic dissection of the traits affecting wheat GY under HS is essential to understand the genetic and molecular basis of HS tolerance. Such analysis will identify the yield component traits most affected by HS. Information generated from these analyses may ameliorate the ways of breeding wheat varieties for HS tolerance.

Few studies have been conducted to identify quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for traits associated with HS tolerance in wheat. Taking GY as a complex trait being affected by HS, QTL mapping was conducted for GY, 1000‐grain weight, days to heading, and grain filling duration by Tura et al. (2020). Using doubled haploid (DH) population, a total of 128 QTLs were found for the four related traits. Eight QTLs for timely sown, 13 for late sown (LS), and 13 for heat susceptibility index (HSI) were mapped using a 35k single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array on a recombinant inbred line (RIL) panel of 238 lines (Singh et al., 2025). These QTLs were detected for GY and its component traits like grain filling duration, grain weight/spike, grain number/spike, grain filling rate, and 1000‐grain weight. Using a backcross inbred lines population of 134 lines evaluated under LS and very late sown (VLS) conditions and genotyped using 95 simple sequence repeat (SSR) markers, Raveendran et al. (2020) identified nine QTLs for various agronomic traits on seven wheat chromosomes. Using a cutoff of logarithm of odds (LOD) 2.5, four QTLs for days to heading, normalized difference vegetative index (NDVI), biomass, and GY were found under LS conditions, and five QTLs for days to heading, NDVI, and spike length (SL) were found under VLS conditions. With an LOD score ranging from 3.03 to 21.01, 24 QTLs were identified for GY, grain number per spike, grain weight per spike, 1000‐grain weight, grain filling rate, and grain filling duration by mapping 52 SSR markers on 251 RILs (Bhusal et al., 2017). Of these, nine QTLs were found under timely sown conditions, six under LS conditions, and nine for HSI of the traits. In the studies cited above, the number of markers used for QTL analysis was relatively small and did not cover the entire wheat genome uniformly. Twelve candidate genes for maximum quantum efficiency were identified for photosystem II by Sharma et al. (2017) using three different F2 populations developed using a common female parent and mapped using 1800 DArTseq (where DArT is diversity array technology) markers. The HS was given under controlled conditions for 3 days at 40°C (day/night) around anthesis. The relationship of the maximum quantum efficiency with any of the agronomic traits under HS was not established.

In another study, mixed model‐based composite interval mapping was performed on a population of 167 RILs evaluated under normal and LS conditions and mapped with 211 amplified fragment length polymorphisms (AFLPs), 120 SSRs, and 144 DArT markers (Hassan et al., 2018). A total of 73 QTLs were identified for GY, proline content, water soluble carbohydrates, maximum efficiency of photosystem II, cytoplasmic membrane stability, and chlorophyll content, of which 37 were identified under normal sown conditions and 36 under LS conditions. As often seen with DArT and AFLP markers, there was severe clustering of markers, and the total map length was about half of what is normally observed in wheat. Two other studies identified QTLs for HSI (Mason et al., 2010), thylakoid membrane damage, SPAD (soil‐plant analysis development) chlorophyll content, and plasma membrane damage (Talukder et al., 2014) by evaluating relatively smaller RIL populations under flash HS treatment for 3–10 days and mapped with a combination of 91 SSRs, 391 bins, and 78 AFLP markers. A direct link of the studied traits to agronomic traits was not established, and the conversion of AFLPs and some of the SSRs into breeder‐friendly markers is difficult.

A population of 148 RILs, including a mixture of lines at different generations (F5, F6, and F7) of the same cross, was used to map QTLs for HSI of 1000‐grain weight, grain filling duration, GY, canopy temperature depression, and days to maturity (Paliwal et al., 2012). The experiment was conducted over 2 years under normal and very late planting conditions, and QTL analysis was performed using 160 SSR markers. In another study, QTL mapping for staygreen‐related traits was conducted using a population of 167 RILs mapped with 118 SSR, 212 AFLP, and 145 DArT markers (Pinto et al., 2016). The experiment was conducted over 5 years, and based on the mean temperature at a particular developmental stage, heat treatment was designated as moderately hot, hot, and intensely hot. A large study involving evaluation of 1413 DH lines from seven populations under controlled conditions at 36°C for 8 h a day for 3 days after anthesis was performed to identify QTLs for the overall performance (Telfer et al., 2021). The study reported QTLs with LOD score as less as 1.9. HS under a controlled environment was also screened by Vijayalakshmi et al. (2010) to map senescence‐related traits in a population of 101 RILs and by Yang et al. (2002) to map QTLs for grain filling duration using F1, F2, and F3 populations. A constant HS was given to the plants at 30°C/25°C (day/night) from 10 days after anthesis till maturity but only 222 and 59 polymorphic markers were used in the two studies. A DH population of 138 lines screened under normal and late planting and genotyped with 205 SSR markers identified QTLs for HIS of traits, of which 13 were identified under normal planting and nine under late planting (Tiwari et al., 2013).

Chromosomal regions controlling various GY‐related traits under HS were also identified via genome wide association mapping using a 280K SNP chip (Touzy et al., 2022). The authors evaluated 199 wheat varieties under controlled condition HS at 29°C/23°C (day/night), 3 days after anthesis, for a period of 10 days. Two regions, one each on chromosomes 4B and 6B, were identified as controlling 1000‐kernel weight. However, none of the studies mentioned above have reported underlying candidate genes in these chromosomal intervals mapped for various studied traits. Since the mapped intervals vary, the availability of the underlying gene(s) can help in devising better breeding strategies.

The objectives of this study were to identify QTLs and the underlying candidate genes involving a cross between a mega‐variety from South‐East Asia and a recently identified wheat line carrying very high level of HS tolerance both under field as well as controlled conditions screening. For accurate QTL detection, a DH population was used that was evaluated under two types of HS in the field along with the non‐stressed condition and was genotyped via a sequencing‐based genotyping (SBG) that is designed to enrich sequences of the genic fraction of the wheat genome.

sec.title: Plant material
sec.p: A mapping population of 196 DH lines was developed from the F1 of a cross between KSG0057 (heat susceptible) and KSG1190 (heat tolerant). The KSG0057 line is a selection out of a CIMMYT line (http://wheatpedigree.net/sort/show/79183) with pedigree of Nord‐Desprez/VG9144//Kalyan Sona/Bluebird/3/Yaco(SIB)/4/Veery#5 that was released under different names in different South‐East Asian countries. In India, it was released as PBW343 by Punjab Agricultural University in the year 1995. KSG1190 is a selection out of an Australian cv. Sunstar that was found to be highly heat tolerant after screening ∼1200 carefully selected wheat lines under five different controlled condition heat screening protocols and 2 years of field testing at five locations in India (Gill et al., unpublished data). Sunstar with pedigree Condor/4∗W15/3/Steinwedel/WC356//La Prevision, was developed by the University of Sydney, Australia. Significant variation was observed among seeds of these two lines thus single plant selections were made and were named KSG0057 and KSG1190. The DH population was developed at Washington State University, Pullman via the wheat × maize hybridization system (Laurie & Bennett, 1988).

sec.title: Phenotypic evaluation of the mapping population
sec.p: Field evaluation of the 196 DH lines along with the two parental lines repeated twice in each replication, was performed using the alpha lattice design. The trial consisted of four replications, each having 10 incomplete blocks of 20 plots each. The recommended seed rate was used to sow each genotype in four rows of 2 m with row‐to‐row spacing of 20 cm. The DH population along with the parents was evaluated for the effect of terminal HS on yield and its component traits at two locations, namely, Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana (30.9010° N, 75.8071° E), and Chaudhary Charan Singh Haryana Agricultural University, Hisar (29.1504° N, 75.7057° E) for 2 years during 2016–2017 and 2017–2018. To assess the effect of high temperature during flowering and grain developmental stages, the trial was conducted on three planting dates. Planting around November 15 as a control, December 15 represents mild HS, whereas planting around January 15 represents severe heat stress (SHS) during flowering and grain filling stages.

The field was irrigated as per the recommendations of the package of practices for wheat. Fifty‐five kilograms of diammonium phosphate (18% N and 46% P2O5) used as a source of P2O5 and 25 kg of urea (46% N) fertilizer was applied just before sowing and the remaining 90 kg of urea was applied in two equal splits with first and second irrigations. The crop was protected from stripe rust by spraying Tilt 25EC (propiconazole) at the rate of 200 mL in 200 L of water per acre for three times at an interval of 2 weeks. Data were recorded on various agronomic traits, including plant height (PH), spike length (SL), number of spikelets per main spike (NSMS), number of grains per main spike (NGMS), 100‐grain weight (HGW), grain weight of main spike (GWMS), and total grain yield (GY). The weekly weather data of the wheat cropping season during 2016–2017 and 2017–2018 for Ludhiana and Hisar were obtained from the agrometeorological department of the Punjab Agricultural University and Chaudhary Charan Singh Haryana Agricultural University, respectively (data not shown). The maximum and minimum temperatures during the heading stage of the DH population were used to plot weather graphs (Figure 1). The graphs were plotted using Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, 2024).

sec.title: Statistical analysis of phenotypic data
sec.p: The descriptive statistics (mean, range, coefficient of variation, and skewness) for all the traits were estimated in individual environment using Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, 2024) and the broad sense heritability (H 2) was calculated using the variability package of R software (R Core Team, 2024). The software MiniTab was used to plot the frequency distribution histograms of the traits. Pearson's correlation coefficients (r) between different traits were determined using the mean data of normal, late, and very late planting obtained during year 1 and year 2 at the two locations. The correlation coefficients were calculated using the agricolae package of the R software (R Core Team, 2024). Regression analysis of the mean data of three planting dates obtained at both the locations during 2 years was done using Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, 2024), and scatter plots of dependent variable (GY) were plotted against independent variables using OPSTAT (https://opstat.pythonanywhere.com/).

sec.title: Reduction percentages
sec.p: The values of reduction percentages of all the traits under study were estimated for both the parents and the DH population using Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Corporation, 2024). The reduction percentage values were estimated for each year and location separately. The reduction percentage values under LS conditions were calculated over the values under normal sown conditions, which represent mild HS for various traits. sec.title: DNA extraction, genotyping, and SNP calling
sec.p: Genomic DNA of the 196 DH lines and the two parents was extracted from 2‐ to 4‐week‐old seedlings using a modified cetyltrimethylammonium bromide method (Randhawa et al., 2009). The quantity and the quality of the DNA were determined by size separating it on a 0.8% agarose gel electrophoresis in the presence of Lambda DNA, used both as a size and concentration marker. DNA concentration was normalized to ∼100 ng/µL. Sequencing‐based genotyping (SBG) was performed by GeneShifters LLC, Pullman (www.geneshifters.com) using their proprietary SBG method. The method specifically enriches sequence for the genic fraction of the genome. Compared to 1%–3% genic fraction that is typically observed in randomly sequenced reactions of wheat samples, the genic fraction of the sequences generated with this method is 23%–29%, as was also seen in the present study. Library preparation, quality check, and sequencing were performed by Geneshifters LLC using their proprietary approach. For sequence data analysis, raw sequencing data were demultiplexed using the barcode splitter program (Hannon, 2010). Individual raw reads of the parental genotype (KSG0057) were aligned to the IWGSC high‐confidence wheat gene annotation version_2 using the bowtie2 mapping program at the default settings (Langmead & Salzberg, 2012; The International Wheat Genome Sequencing Consortium (IWGSC) et al., 2018). Duplicate reads were removed and a consensus sequence for the mapped reads was developed using the CAP3 program (Huang & Madan, 1999). The de novo consensus sequence of the parental genotype was used to map reads of the DH population and the donor line (KSG1190) using the bowtie2 mapping program (Langmead & Salzberg, 2012). SNP calling was done using the VCFtools program, and the SNPs with more than 80% allele call and a minimum sequencing depth of 10 reads were retained for further analysis (Danecek et al., 2011). SNP call data were sorted based on the wheat physical reference genome and were converted to A (KSG0057), B (KSG1190), and H (Heterozygous) format using the standalone tassel package (Bradbury et al., 2007). This analysis provided 5307 SNP markers to be used for the construction of a linkage map.

sec.title: Linkage map construction
sec.p: The 674 SNPs showing polymorphism between the two parents and showing less than 20% missing data were used to develop the genetic linkage map. A linkage map was constructed using the MSTmap package in R studio. Kosambi (1944) mapping function was used to construct the map with genetic distance allowed between markers set at 20 cM with an LOD score of 3.

sec.title: QTL discovery
sec.p: The genetic linkage map obtained as described in the previous section was used to find the QTLs for various traits. The QTL analyses for planting dates over the years, locations, dates, and reduction percentages were individually done using Windows QTL cartographer v2.5 (Wang et al.,2012) (http://statgen.ncsu.edu/qtlcart/WQTLCart.htm). Initially, single marker analysis (SMA) was done to find the SNP markers associated with the phenotypic traits. Default parameters were used to find the marker trait association and a QTL with an LOD score of 2.5 at a 5% level of significance was considered as a putative QTL. Composite interval mapping (CIM) (Jiang & Zeng, 1995; Zeng, 1994) was then performed at a walk speed of 2 cM to determine the likely position of the QTL on the linkage group. The co‐factors for CIM were selected following the standard model (model 6) and forward and backward method of regression at 10 cM window size, taking five markers at a time at p = 0.1. LOD threshold score for each trait was calculated using 1000 permutation test at significance level of p = 0.05 (Churchill & Doerge, 1994; Doerge & Churchill, 1996). The LOD score of >2.5 was also considered for the detection of putative QTLs. The QTLs identified were designated based on the International Rules of Genetic Nomenclature (https://wheat.pw.usda.gov/ggpages/wgc/98/Intro.htm), which is comprised of a “Q” followed by trait name, a period, laboratory designation, a hyphen, and the chromosome assignment. The QTL with the highest phenotypic variance was considered as the most significant QTL and the QTL present in the multiple environments was considered as the consistent QTL.

sec.title: Assignment of physical locations to the QTLs
sec.p: The gene (coding sequence) sequence of the markers flanking each of the QTL‐containing intervals was retrieved using the Gene ID from Ensembl Plants wheat (https://plants.ensembl.org/index.html). These sequences were used to determine the physical location of the QTLs on the genome. The gene sequences of the flanking markers were used to find their homoeologous and paralogous genes present on the same or different chromosomes by subjecting them to blastn against the IWGSC reference genome on Ensembl Plants wheat (https://plants.ensembl.org/Triticum_aestivum/Tools/Blast) following the default settings. The physical locations of the sequences with similarity percentage of more than 85% and a query coverage of more than 100 bp present on the same chromosome were noted, and the smallest region confined by the flanking markers was assigned as the physical location of the QTL on the chromosome. For the QTLs flanked with the common marker, copies and physical locations of the marker were found as described above. The location of the selected coordinates was confirmed by ensuring presence of the flanking markers for the regions.

sec.title: Identification of the candidate genes for the QTLs
sec.p: The number of candidate genes present in each QTL‐containing region was found using the BIOMART window of the Ensembl Plants (https://plants.ensembl.org/biomart/martview), selecting the appropriate filters of assembly to be used for comparison, chromosome number, and start and end positions along with the gene ID.

sec.title: Phenotypic evaluation of the DH population
sec.p: Based on the phenotypic data collected on various plant and grain traits, significant variation was observed between the parents on different dates of sowing, locations, and years (Table 1). Among locations, years, and planting dates, the GY of KSG0057 ranged 3.8 times (344–1317.50 g) compared to 4.3 times (226–964 g) for KSG1190. On an average, yields were higher during 2017–2018 as compared to that during 2016–2017. Comparing different planting dates, expectedly yields were the highest under the normal sowing (NS) condition, followed by the LS and then VLS conditions. KSG0057 showed the highest yield under normal sown condition at Hisar location during 2016–2017, whereas KSG1190 gave the highest yield under LS planting at Hisar during 2017–2018. Both parents showed the lowest yield under VLS planting at Hisar during 2016–2017.

sec.p: The HGW also showed variation between the two parents, among different planting dates, and between the 2 years, but the extent was not as much as observed for GY (Table 1). With an average of 3.53 g, HGW for KSG0057 ranged from 4.44 to 2.44 g (1.8 times) as compared to 3.37 to 1.89 g (1.8 times) for KSG1190, which showed a mean of 2.72 g. While maximum reduction in HGW was observed for VLS planting, very little difference was observed between NS and LS plantings with some cases of higher HGW during LS conditions (Table 1). Similar to GY, the maximum HGW for both the parents was recorded under normal sown conditions and the minimum during the VLS conditions.

The mean of GWMS for KSG0057 under NS was 2.15 g with a range from 1.90 to 2.48 g, under LS was 1.78 g with a range from 1.52 to 2.00 g, and under VLS was 1.30 g with a range from 1.06 to 1.52 g. KSG1190 had a mean of 1.75 g with a range from 1.68 to 1.90 g for GWMS under NS, 1.39 g with a range from 1.21 to 1.52 g under LS, and 1.09 g with a range from 0.91 to 1.40 g under VLS. For KSG0057, the average GWMS was higher during 2016–2017, whereas KSG1190 had shown the high average during 2017–2018. KSG1190 has shown either equal or higher value of NGMS than KSG0057 in all the test environments except under VLS conditions in Ludhiana during 2017–2018. With an average of 46.85, NGMS for KSG0057 varied between 38.40 and 59.38 (1.5 times), whereas for KSG1190, it ranged from 38.67 to 61.53 (1.5 times) with an average of 49.40. Overall, for both parents, the NGMS was the highest under NS and the lowest during VLS (Table 1).

For the NSMS, KSG1190 was either slightly less or better than KSG0057 in all the environments. For both parents, NSMS was similar with KSG1190 having slight advantage, and values were less variable (1.1 times for both parents) over replications, years, and location as compared to the other traits. During 2016–2017, the average for KSG0057 was 19.58 as compared to 20.38 for KSG1190. The difference between the parents was similar, although the average was slightly higher during 2017–2018. The SL was highly variable over locations, years, and planting times (Table 1). With SL of 11.52 cm for KSG0057 and 10.29 cm for KSG1190, both the parents showed the longest SL during 2016–2017. During 2017–2018, the average SL of KSG1190 under VLS (9.6 cm) was higher than NS (9.4 cm) and LS (8.2 cm). With the average PH of 82.12 cm for KSG0057 and 74.40 cm for KSG1190, KSG0057 had 10.37% higher PH than KSG1190 and it did not change much over the years or the locations. PH in both parents was lower during LS and VLS planting, and the reduction was 18.62% in KSG0057 as compared to 19.36% in KSG1190.

For all the studied traits, the DH lines showed tremendous variation with transgressive segregation in both directions (Table 1; Figure 2). The pattern of higher trait values during NS and the lowest during VLS planting that was observed for the two parents was consistent for the DH lines as well. With a mean of 584.52 g per plot, GY for the DH lines ranged from 63 to 1423.75 g (22.6 times difference). SL showed the least variation among DH lines with a range from 5.89 to 12.79 cm (2.2 times). The range among the DH lines for other traits was 1.43–4.65 g (3.3 times) for HGW, 0.45–2.80 g (6.2 times) for GWMS, 15.60–76.95 (4.9 times) for NGMS, 15.00–35.91 (2.4 times) for NSMS, and 50.07–133.90 cm (2.7 times) for PH.

sec.p: While distribution of the DH lines for various traits and conditions (planting dates and locations) was normal with few exceptions, significant differences were observed for the distribution over different planting dates (Table 1). In eight of the 12 environments, GY was skewed toward KSG1190. During 2016–2017 under LS conditions at Ludhiana, it was normally distributed, whereas under NS in Ludhiana and VLS at Hisar, it was skewed toward KSG0057 during both years. Under all four environments of VLS, the DH population was skewed toward KSG0057 for HGW. The results for HGW holds true for GWMS except under VLS at Hisar during 2017–2018. The distribution among DH lines for the NGMS was skewed toward KSG1190 across all of the environments. In comparison, skewness for NSMS toward KSG1190 was seen only under VLS conditions except in Ludhiana during 2017–2018. The DH population distribution was fairly normal for SL, whereas the distribution of PH was skewed toward KSG0057 in all the studied environments. With 27.73%, GY showed the maximum mean coefficient of variation across all the environments, whereas SL showed the minimum coefficient of variation value of 7.40%. The broad sense heritability of the traits ranged from 0.66 for PH to 0.43 for SL and NGMS.

The extent of transgressive segregation was highly variable among traits (Figure 2). The NSMS was similar between the two parents but the DH population showed tremendous transgressive segregation both in the positive as well as in the negative direction. On the other hand, transgressive segregation was much less for GY and HGW. For some traits, including HGW and GY, transgressive segregation was mainly in the negative direction, especially in the normal planting conditions. There were significant differences for the distribution pattern and transgressive segregation among traits, planting times, and locations. Negative transgressive segregation for GY was significantly higher for normal planting as compared to very late planting. At the Hisar location, GWMS showed relatively uniform distribution containing transgressive segregation in both directions. At Ludhiana, however, most of the transgressive segregation was in the negative direction. Other traits, including NSMS, showed very similar distribution pattern between locations.

sec.title: Reduction percentages
sec.p: In order to analyze the HS tolerance of parents and the DH population, reduction percentages of LS from NS (termed as HS tolerance), VLS from NS (termed as SHS tolerance), and VLS from LS (termed as the difference between the two types of HS) were calculated for all the traits, years, and locations (Table 2). For GY, the reduction percentages among the DH plants in different environments ranged from −5.25% to 59.82%. For the two parents, the range for KSG0057 was from −16.95% to 73.93% as compared to −24.16% to 72.89% for KSG1190. Similarly, for HGW, the reduction percentage range for DH lines was from −3.04% to 33.42% in comparison to −3.45% to 42.81% for KSG0057 and 1.50% to 37.50% for KSG1190. The mean reduction percentages for the DH lines for GWMS (26.30%) were very similar to the mean of the two parents (26.62%). Similarly, the average of reduction percentages of DH lines for NGMS was 13.10% with a range of −5.62% to 27.06%; for NSMS it was 9.44% with a range of −0.32% to 28.59%; for SL it was 5.19% with a range of −7.88% to 16.99%; and for PH it was 11.48% with a range between 1.97% and 16.79%.

sec.title: Correlation and regression analysis
sec.p: Pearson's correlation coefficients were determined for each trait and were compared between the 2 years and two locations (Table 3; Figure S1). GY showed significant positive correlation with HGW and GWMS. HGW showed significant negative correlation with NGMS and NSMS. NSMS also had negative correlations with GY, HGW, and GWMS. In general, correlation coefficients between traits were more similar between the 2 years of the same location as compared to the correlation coefficients between the two locations, although some differences were observed.

sec.p: Considered as an independent variable, regression of other traits was studied on GY, and the results are given in Table S1 and Figure S2. As expected, both HGW and GWMS showed strong positive regression on GY. On the other hand, PH, SL, and NGMS had very little effect on GY. NSMS had a negative effect on GY. In general, regression pattern did not change much over the years and locations barring some differences. For example, regression of HGW was much higher during 2017–2018 as compared to that of the previous year.

sec.title: Genetic linkage map
sec.p: Using SBG, ∼200 million reads were generated for the population, with an average of 1 million reads per sample. An average of ∼200,000 reads per sample represented the genic fraction. After initial mapping, aligned reads were assembled using the CAP3 program to develop a custom reference genome of the parents of the DH population to identify ∼5000 bi‐allelic SNPs for the DH population. Using a minimum sequencing depth of 10 reads per SNP (see Section 2) and less than 20% missing data, 674 high‐quality SNP markers were identified and used for QTL analysis and linkage map construction, which revealed a total length of 3875.31 cM for the 21 wheat chromosomes. The average genetic distance between the two markers was 5.75 cM, with 32.1 markers on each chromosome, whereas the average physical distance between the two markers was 25.2 Mb. Across the three sub‐genomes of wheat, the highest marker density and genetic length were observed for the D‐genome with 270 markers and 1449.3 cM genetic length, followed by the B‐genome having 229 markers distributed on a total genetic length of 1276.6 cM. The genetic length across the A‐genome was 1149.4 cM with 175 markers. Out of the 21 chromosomes, 7B had the longest linkage map of 294.8 cM with 51 markers, whereas the highest number of markers (57) were mapped on the 5D chromosome. Similarly, 4B had the lowest number of markers (14) on a length of 64.1 cM.

sec.title: QTL analysis
sec.p: CIM (Section 2) performed individually for different locations, years, and planting dates identified 66 chromosomal regions that contained 155 QTLs for GY, HGW, GWMS, NGMS, NSMS, SL, and PH (Table 4; Figure S3). These 66 regions were present on 15 of the 21 wheat chromosomes with chromosomes 3D, 4B, 4D, 5B, 6D, and 7A not having any of the QTL‐containing regions. The maximum number of 12 regions was found on chromosome 2B. Surprisingly, eight of the 12 2B regions were present on the short arm. Chromosome 1B had only one region.

sec.p: Of the 66 chromosomal regions, 33 had only one QTL each, 15 regions had two QTLs each, and each of the remaining 18 had more than two QTLs. The maximum number of QTLs was seven present in a region present on chromosome 2DL. In general, the QTLs present in the same region had positive contribution by the same parent with few exceptions.

sec.title: QTLs for GY
sec.p: The highest number of QTLs among the studied traits was 27 detected for GY located on 1A, 1D, 2B, 2D, 3A, 3B, 5D, 6B, 7B, and 7D (Table 4; Figure S3). QTLs on 1D, 2B, 2D, 3A, 3B, 6B, 7B, and 7D were co‐localized with QTLs for other traits, including HGW, GWMS, NGMS, NSMS, SL, and PH. The remaining QTLs were present individually in the corresponding regions. Out of the 27 QTLs, KSG0057 had positive contribution for 18 and KSG1190 had positive contribution for the remaining nine QTLs.

Evaluating across the planting dates, eight yield QTLs were detected under NS, two under LS, and 11 QTLs under VLS. One QTL each present on chromosomes 2BL and 2DL was detected under all three planting times. One QTL present on 7D was detected under NS and VLS conditions, and three QTLs on 2B, 3A, and 7D were detected under LS and VLS conditions. Eight QTLs, three on 2B, one each on chromosomes 2D, 3A, and 7B, and two on 7D, were detected only under VLS conditions at the Ludhiana location, whereas eight QTLs located on 1D, 2B, 2D, 3A, 6B, 7B, and 7D were detected under the VLS conditions at the Hisar location. The two locations were very different as none of the QTLs detected under VLS planting were common to the two locations. Overall, three QTLs were common for both locations, 16 were found only for the Ludhiana location and eight were only for the Hisar location. Comparing the QTLs over the years, six QTLs were detected over both years, 13 only during year 1 and eight only during year 2.

Analyzed with 1000 permutations, the LOD score for the GY QTLs ranged from 2.50, which was used as a cutoff, to 10.06 (given in Table 4). Twelve of the GY QTLs had an LOD value > 3 and five had >5. Seven QTLs present on 2B, 2D, 3A, and 7D chromosomes appeared in more than one environment and had a range of LOD value between 4.49 and 10.06, 3.27 and 4.82, 2.72 and 3.58, 2.59 and 6.52, 4.24 and 4.51, 2.83 and 3.03, and 4.52 and 5.57. So, the upper value of LOD and phenotypic variance explained (PVE) was taken to classify the QTLs with LOD value > 3 or 5 and PVE > 20% or 30%. For example, the 3A QTL (QGY.pau‐3AS.1) having an LOD score of 2.59–6.52 explaining 13.45%–31.21% of the phenotypic variance was classified as the QTL having an LOD score >5 and PVE > 30%. With a range of 5.60%–62.76%, three of the GY QTLs explained more than 20% of the phenotypic variance and six explained more than 30% in the respective environment. The most significant (defined above) GY QTL was QGY.pau‐2BS.3 found with an LOD score of 9.44 and explaining 62.76% of the phenotypic variance. QGY.pau‐2BS.1 was co‐localized with other important traits, including HGW and GWMS, with a significantly higher LOD score of 6.67. This QTL was explaining the trait with 59.78% phenotypic variance. QGY.pau‐2BL.4 was the most consistent (defined in Section 2) GY QTL detected under all the three planting conditions. The LOD score of this QTL varied from 2.72 to 3.58 with PVE ranging between 14.66% and 18.74%.

The size of the regions containing the GY QTLs ranged from 1.59 kb to 155.91 Mb (Table 4). Five of these regions are smaller than 100 kb and seven are smaller than 5 Mb. Number of candidate genes in these regions ranged from 1 to 1750 with an average of 210 genes per region. Five of these regions containing QGY.pau‐1AL.2, QGY.pau‐1DL.2, QGY.pau‐2BL.4, QGY.pau‐3AL.3, and QGY.pau‐7DL.4 QTLs have only one candidate gene each. The QTL regions of the QGY.pau‐6BS.1 and QGY.pau‐7BL.1 had two and four candidate genes, respectively.

sec.title: QTLs for HGW
sec.p: Eighteen QTLs were detected for HGW, of which nine were located on chromosome 2B, two each on 2D, 3A, 3B, and 7B, and one on 1D (Table 4; Figure S3). Of these, two QTLs were detected under NS conditions, four under LS, and 11 under VLS. One QTL was detected under both LS and VLS conditions. Most of the HGW QTLs were found to be co‐localized with the QTLs for GWMS or NGMS. Nine of the HGW QTLs on chromosomes 2B, 2D, 3A, 3B, and 7B were co‐localized with the GY QTLs. Of the 18 QTLs, 13 had positive alleles from KSG0057, and the four QTLs present on 2B and one on 1D showed positive alleles from KSG1190. The 2D QTLs were specific to VLS conditions, and those on 2B were detected both under LS and VLS conditions. Of the 18 QTLs, two were detected over both years and 16 were observed only during one of the 2 years. Comparison of locations showed that three QTLs were detected for both locations, whereas the remaining QTLs were detected at only one of the two locations. Two QTLs of HGW on 2B chromosome and one on 7B chromosome were detected under VLS conditions at both the locations.

Analyzed with 1000 permutations, 15 of the 18 HGW QTLs were detected with an LOD score of >5. There were three QTLs with phenotypic variance >20% and 12 QTLs showed the phenotypic variance >30% in the corresponding environment. The most significant QTL for HGW (QHGW.pau‐2BL.8) was detected with an LOD score of >5 and explained >30% of the trait under VLS conditions of both the locations. The QTL, QHGW.pau‐7BL.2, with an LOD score of 2.73–6.0 explained 17.93%–38.16% of the phenotypic variance and was the most consistent QTL of HGW detected under VLS conditions at both the locations. The QTL was co‐localized with the QTLs for GY, GWMS, NGMS, NSMS, SL, and PH.

The size of the HGW QTL‐containing regions ranged from 136.7 kb to 78.73 Mb (Table 4). The smallest regions of 136.7 kb on 2B chromosome had only one candidate gene. Two other regions smaller than 0.84 Mb had less than 10 candidate genes.

sec.title: QTLs for GWMS
sec.p: The 23 QTLs found for GWMS were located on chromosomes 1B, 1D, 2B, 2D, 3A, 3B, 4A, 6B, and 7B (Table 4; Figure S3). Of these, 17 were co‐localized with NGMS and other traits. KSG1190 provided the positive alleles for 12 GWMS QTLs and KSG0057 for the remaining 11 QTLs. Six of the GWMS QTLs were specific to NS, five for LS, and nine for VLS conditions. One each QTL was detected for the NS and LS, NS and VLS, and LS and VLS conditions. There were 14 QTLs specific to year 1 and seven specific to year 2. There were only two QTLs that were common to the 2 years. Among locations, 12 QTLs were specific for the Ludhiana location and eight for the Hisar location. The remaining three QTLs were common to the two locations. One QTL on 2B and one QTL on 6B were detected under VLS condition at both the locations during 2016–2017.

The LOD score for the GWMS QTLs ranged from 2.60 to 30.53 with eight QTLs having >3 and 10 having >5. The range of phenotypic variance was observed between 11.10% and 76.70%. There were four QTLs of GWMS with PVE >20% and eight QTLs with PVE >30% in their respective environment. The most significant QTL (QGWMS.pau‐2BS.1) for GWMS was present on chromosome 2B with an LOD of 29.05 and phenotypic variance of 76.70%. The most consistent QTL (QGWMS.pau‐2BL.8) was present under multiple environments with an LOD value of 2.82–25.58 and 25.72%–73.47% phenotypic variance.

The size of the GWMS QTL‐containing regions ranged from 7.7 kb to 106.6 Mb (Table 4). Four of the regions were smaller than 100 kb and seven <5 Mb. With a range of 1–826 genes, seven regions contained <10 candidate genes, and the region having QTL, QGWMS.pau‐4AL, was located in a region of 7.7 kb with only one candidate gene.

sec.title: QTLs for NGMS
sec.p: Twenty‐five QTLs were detected for NGMS, of which four were on chromosomes 3 and 4 of the A genome, 15 on chromosomes 2, 3, 6, and 7 of the B genome, and six on chromosomes 2 and 7 of the D genome (Table 4; Figure S3). Out of the 25 QTLs, nine were present on chromosome 2B and five on 2D. Of the 25, 23 QTLs for NGMS were co‐localized with that for other traits, including GY, GWMS, and PH. KSG0057 made positive contribution to 19 of the QTLs and KSG1190 to the remaining six.

Of the NGMS QTLs, three were specific for NS, one for LS, and 16 under VLS conditions. Five of the QTLs were common to both LS and VLS conditions. For years, 14 QTLs were specific to year 1 and eight to year 2. There were three QTLs that were common to both years. Comparison among locations revealed nine QTLs to be specific for Ludhiana, 10 for Hisar, and six QTLs were common between the two locations. Three QTLs, two present on 2B and one present on 6B chromosome were detected under VLS conditions at both Ludhiana and Hisar.

Of the 25 NGMS QTLs, 10 were detected with >3 LOD score and 13 with >5. Six QTLs showed >20% phenotypic variance and 12 with >30% in the corresponding environment. The most significant QTL, QNGMS.pau‐3AS.2, was detected under two environments with 26.84 and 55.73 LOD score explaining 74.98% and 85.44% of the trait variation. There were two most consistent QTLs present on 2B chromosome (QNGMS.pau‐2B.6 and QNGMS.pau‐2B.8), which appeared under multiple environments with LOD score ranging between 4.80–47.72 and 35.88–57.58. The PVE by these QTLs had a range from 39.30% to 81.35% and 72.20% to 81.35%.

The size of the NGMS QTL‐containing regions ranged from 8.9 kb to 89.2 Mb (Table 4). Four of the NGMS QTL‐containing regions were smaller than 100 kb and seven smaller than 5 Mb. With a range of 1–791 genes, seven QTL‐containing regions had <10 candidate genes. A region on 2B and one on chromosome 7B had only one candidate gene each.

sec.title: QTLs for NSMS
sec.p: Of the 18 QTLs identified for NSMS, five were present on chromosome 2B and three on 2D (Table 4; Figure S3). All of the NSMS QTLs were co‐localized with QTLs for other traits except for the one present on chromosome 5D. KSG0057 provided positive allele for the QTLs present on chromosomes 2B, 2D, 3A, and 6A chromosomes, whereas KSG1190 provided the positive alleles for the QTLs present on 1D, 5A, 5D, and 6B. The positive alleles for the QTLs present on 7B were contributed by both the parents.

Comparison of the three planting dates identified one QTL to be specific for NS, four for LS, and 12 for VLS conditions. There was one QTL that was common to NS and VLS conditions. Between the years, seven QTLs were specific to the year 1, eight were specific to the year 2, and three were common to both years. Between locations, three QTLs were specific to Ludhiana location, eight to Hisar location, and seven QTLs were common between the two locations. There were four QTLs detected common to both the locations under VLS conditions. The QTLs were present on 2B, 2D, and 6B chromosomes.

The NSMS QTLs showed an LOD score of >2.51 and a phenotypic variance of >6.99%. There were three QTLs with LOD >3 and 11 with >5. With regard to phenotypic variance, two QTLs showed the PVE of >20% and 10 showed >30% in the corresponding environment. The best QTL (QNSMS.pau‐3AS.1) present on chromosome 3A had an LOD value of 88.72 and a phenotypic variance of 90.32%. QTL present on 2B, QNSMS.pau‐2BS.3, was detected under VLS conditions of both the locations with an LOD score >5 and PVE >30%. Another QTL, QNSMS.pau‐7BL.2, was detected in three environments, showed an LOD score range between 3.09 and 4.36 and phenotypic variance from 13.39% to 22.89%.

The size of the regions containing NSMS QTLs ranged from 8.9 kb to 89.2 Mb and contained 1–791 genes (Table 4). Four of these regions were <100 kb and another two were <5 Mb. The smallest region contained QTL, QNSMS.pau‐7BL.3 in 8.9 kb and had only one candidate gene. QTLs, QNSMS.pau‐3AL.2 and QNSMS.pau‐6BS, were located in the regions of 18.7 and 14.9 kb with two candidate genes each.

sec.title: QTLs for SL
sec.p: Twenty‐three QTLs, one each on chromosomes 1B and 2A; two on 1A, 2D, 5A, 6A, and 7B; three on 6B; and four on chromosomes 2B and 3A were located for SL (Table 4; Figure S3). Sixteen of the 23 SL QTLs were co‐located with the QTLs of other traits. KSG0057 contributed positive allele for 16 of the QTLs of SL and KSG1190 contributed for the remaining seven.

Comparison of the planting dates, four of the SL QTLs were specific for NS and LS conditions each and 10 were specific for VLS. Four QTLs were common between NS and LS and one between LS and VLS conditions. Between the years, 10 QTLs were specific for the year 1, five for the year 2, and eight QTLs were common for 2 years. Between locations, five SL QTLs were specific for Ludhiana, eight for the Hisar location, and 10 QTLs were common to the two locations. One QTL present each on 2B, 2D, and 6B chromosomes and two QTLs on 7B chromosome were detected under VLS conditions at both the locations.

Of the 23 QTLs for SL, seven were detected with an LOD score of >3 and another 13 had an LOD value >5. With reference to phenotypic variance, there were six QTLs with PVE >20% and nine with >30% in their corresponding environment. The most significant QTL present on 3A, QSL.pau‐3AS.3, was found in three environments with an LOD value of 52.25–93.84 explaining 78.37%–87.68% of the phenotypic variation. The QTL was also co‐located with the QTLs of HGW, GWMS, NGMS, NSMS, and PH. Another significant and consistent QTL, QSL.pau‐5AL.1, present on 5A was detected in three environments with an LOD score ranging from 2.51 to 5.90, explaining 8.39%–22.83% of the phenotypic variation.

The size range of the SL QTL‐containing regions ranged from 2.9 kb to 92.1 Mb (Table 4). The smallest region of 2.9 kb present on chromosome 5A contained only one candidate gene. The size of another three regions was <100 kb. The number of candidate gene in the QTL‐containing regions of SL varied between 1 and 606 with an average of 130 genes. The two SL QTL‐containing regions present on chromosomes 2B and 5A had only one candidate gene. Another four regions had less than 10 candidate genes.

sec.title: QTLs for PH
sec.p: Among the 21 QTLs found for PH, seven were present on chromosome 2B, three on 7B, two each on 2D, 3A, and 5A, and one each on chromosomes 1A, 1D, 6B, and 7D (Table 4; Figure S3). Of the 21 QTLs, 18 were co‐localized with the QTLs for the other traits. KSG0057 contributed the positive allele for 15 of the PH QTLs and the remaining six were contributed by KSG1190.

Only one QTL was specific for NS, whereas the number of specific PH QTLs for LS conditions was six and for VLS was 13. The remaining QTL was common for LS and VLS conditions. Between the years, seven QTLs were specific for year 1, 11 were specific for year 2, and two were common between the years. At Hisar, one QTL of PH present on 2B chromosome was detected during both the years. Comparison among locations revealed three QTLs to be specific for Ludhiana, 12 for Hisar, and the remaining six were common. During 2016–2017, a QTL on 5A was detected under NS condition at both the locations and a QTL on 6B was detected under VLS conditions at both the locations. Two QTLs of PH on 2B chromosome and one on 2D chromosome under VLS condition were common between both the locations during 2017–2018.

Of the 21 PH QTLs, 19 had an LOD score >3 and 11 with >5. Thirteen QTLs explained >20% of the phenotypic variance and 10 explained >30% in their respective environment. Co‐localized with many other QTLs, QPH.pau‐3AS.2 was the most significant QTL present in two environments with an LOD score of >5 and phenotypic variance >30%. Another QTL on 6B, QPH.pau6BS, was present under VLS conditions at both the locations during 2016–2017. The QTL had an LOD value of 2.55 and 2.77 explaining 12.60% and 11.86% of the phenotypic variance.

The size of regions containing the PH QTLs ranged from 2.9 kb to 47.0 Mb (Table 4). The size of nine regions was smaller than 5 Mb and for three was <100 kb. The two smallest regions present on chromosomes 2B and 5A had only one candidate gene each. The region on chromosome 6B had two candidate genes and three other regions had <10 candidate genes.

sec.title: QTLs for trait reduction under HS conditions
sec.p: CIM using reduction percentage data (see Section 2) identified 100 chromosomal regions that contained 152 QTLs for the seven traits (Table 4; Figure S3). These QTLs were distributed on all 21 chromosomes with the maximum number of 17 regions present on chromosome 2B. Eleven QTL‐containing regions were present on chromosome 7B. There was only one QTL region present on 1B, 4A, 4B, 5B, and 7D chromosomes.

Of the 100 regions, 69 have only a single QTL, 20 have two, and 11 regions have more than two QTLs. The maximum number of six QTLs was present on chromosomes 2B and 2D. Of these 100, 38 regions were common to those identified using the trait data (described above). In 38 common regions, GY QTLs were found in 10 regions and HGW QTLs were also found to be common in 10 other regions. The traits having least number of common regions between the two analyses were SL and PH. The QTLs of both the traits appeared only under two of the 38 common regions.

sec.title: GY QTLs for heat stress tolerance (HGY)
sec.p: Of the 29 QTLs detected for HGY, 18 co‐located with QTLs of other traits, including HGW, GWMS, NGMS, NSMS, SL, and PH (Table 4; Figure S3). For parental contribution, KSG0057 had positive alleles for 16 QTLs and KSG1190 had them for 11. For the remaining two QTLs, both parents contributed positive alleles over different environments. Eight HGY QTLs were for HS (see Section 2 for description), three for SHS, and 13 for the difference between the two types of HS, including eight present on chromosome 2B. Comparing the years, 10 QTLs were specific for year 1, 18 for year 2, and one was common. For locations, 11 were specific for Ludhiana, 14 for Hisar, and four were common.

Twenty HGY QTLs had an LOD score of >3 and eight had >5. Of these, 12 QTLs had PVE >30% in the corresponding environment. The most significant QTL (QHGY.pau‐2BS.3) for the trait is present on chromosome 2B in two environments, for which PVE is 76.96% and 28.27% with an LOD score of 48.43 and 3.13. The QTL was also co‐located with other important traits like HGW and GWMS. Another example of the consistent QTL is QHGY.pau‐2DL.1, present in multiple environments with the QTLs of HHGW, HGWMS, HNGMS, HNSMS, and HPH. The LOD score of this QTL had a range from 4.09 to 4.75 with PVE ranging from 21.50% to 27.41%.

The size of the QTL‐containing regions ranged from 6.5 kb to 129.2 Mb (Table 4) with five regions smaller than 1 Mb. Number of candidate genes ranged from 1 to 1750 with QHGY.pau‐2BL.6 and QHGY.pau‐2BL.10 containing regions having only one candidate gene each and three others with less than 10.

sec.title: HGW QTLs for heat stress tolerance (HHGW)
sec.p: Twenty‐three QTLs were detected for HHGW, of which 14 co‐located with QTLs for GWMS and other traits (Table 4; Figure S3). Eight of the QTLs were present on the short arm of chromosome 2B. KSG1190 contributed the positive alleles for 13 QTLs and KSG0057 to the remaining 10. Six of the QTLs were for HS and SHS each, and three QTLs were for the difference between the two types of HS. Six of the QTLs were specific for year 1, 16 for year 2, and one was common for both years. While no QTL was common for both locations, 15 were specific for Ludhiana and eight for Hisar.

The LOD score for the HHGW QTLs ranged from 2.55 to 16.07 with six QTLs having LOD >5. The PVE had a range from 1.78% to 68.88% with nine QTLs having PVE >30% in their respective environment. The HHGW QTL present on 2B chromosome, QHHGW.pau‐2BS.8, was the most significant QTL found to be co‐located with QTLs of other important traits, including HGY and HGWMS, in two environments. The LOD score of the QTL in two environments was 9.45 and 16.07 and PVE was 68.88% and 68.56%. Another important QTL on 2D, QHHGW.pau‐2DL.1, was consistently present in multiple environments with an LOD score ranging from 2.76 to 4.80 and explaining PVE with a range from 13.07% to 22.54%. This QTL was also co‐located with the QTLs of HHGY, HGWMS, HNGMS, HNSMS, and HPH.

The size of the QTL‐containing regions varied from 1.8 kb to 89.2 Mb with three regions smaller than 100 kb (Table 4). The number of candidate genes per region ranged from 1 to 791 with the 1.8 kb region containing QHHGW.pau‐7BL.2 and a 51.5 kb region containing QHHGW.pau‐5DL.2 had only one candidate gene each. Two other regions containing QTLs, QHHGW.pau‐2BL.9 and QHHGW.pau‐6BS, have less than 10 candidate genes.

sec.title: GWMS QTLs for heat stress tolerance (HGWMS)
sec.p: Of the 21 QTLs detected for HGWMS, 15 co‐localized with that for other trait QTLs (Table 4; Figure S3). KSG0057 contributed the positive allele for 10 of the QTLs, KSG1190 for eight, and there was an equal contribution of the two parents for the remaining three. The maximum number (14) of the HGWMS QTLs was observed for SHS with one each for HS and the difference between the two types of HS. Between years, 12 QTLs were specific for year 1, six for year 2, and three were common. There were 13 QTLs specific for Ludhiana, seven for Hisar, and one was common to both the locations.

Fourteen HGWMS QTLs were detected with an LOD score of >3 and seven with >5. Nine QTLs explained more than 30% of the phenotypic variance in the corresponding environment. The most significant QTL, QHGWMS.pau‐2BS.7, was identified with an LOD score of 13.02 and PVE of 72.06%. Another significant QTL on 2B, QHGWMS.pau‐2BS.3, was consistently present in multiple environments with QTLs of other traits, including HGY, HHGW, and HNSMS. The LOD score of this QTL had a range from 4.62 to 10.71 and PVE ranging between 59.71% and 72.00%.

The size of the QTL‐containing regions ranged from 156.1 kb to 257.0 Mb with four being smaller than 1 Mb (Table 4). Number of candidate genes in these regions varied between 1 and 1201. The smallest region of 156.1 kb on 2B has five candidate genes. On the other hand, the 198.6 kb region on 5B has only one gene and a 295.7 kb region on 1D has two candidate genes.

sec.title: NGMS QTLs for heat stress tolerance (HNGMS)
sec.p: Of the 22 QTLs identified for HNGMS, 14 were co‐located with HGY and other trait QTLs (Table 4; Figure S3). Except for six QTLs, positive allele was contributed by KSG0057. Five QTLs were detected each for HS and SHS, and nine were for the difference of the two types of HS. Fifteen HNGMS QTLs were specific for year 1, five for year 2, and the remaining two were common. For locations, 11 QTLs were specific for Ludhiana, nine for Hisar, and two were common.

With a range of 2.59–5.39, 16 had an LOD value >3 and three had >5. The range for PVE varied from 8.04% to 47.81% with two QTLs having PVE >30% in the respective environment. A QTL, QNGMS.pau‐4DL.2, was the most significant QTL for HNGMS. The LOD score of this QTL is 3.20 with 47.81% phenotypic variance. The most consistent QTL for HNGMS was detected on chromosome 7B. QNGMS.pau‐3AS.1 was present in multiple environments with the QTLs of HGY, HHGW, and HPH with an LOD score ranging between 2.79 and 4.59 and PVE ranging from 12.41% to 21.28%.

The size of the HNGMS QTL‐containing regions ranged from 247.3 kb to 684.9 Mb with two regions smaller than 1 Mb (Table 4). The number of candidate genes ranged from 2 to 4869 with two regions having less than 10 candidate genes.

sec.title: NSMS QTLs for heat stress tolerance (HNSMS)
sec.p: Twenty‐eight QTLs were identified for HNSMS, of which eight co‐localized with other QTLs (Table 4; Figure S3). For 18 QTLs out of 28, the positive allele for the trait was contributed by KSG0057 and by KSG1190 for the remaining 10 QTLs. There were eight QTLs detected for HS, 12 for SHS, and eight for the difference between the two types of HS. Ten QTLs of HNSMS were specific for year 1 and 18 were specific for year 2. For locations, 16 QTLs were specific for Ludhiana and 12 for Hisar. There was no QTL common between year or location for this trait.

The range of the LOD score varied from 2.5 to 25.82 for HNSMS with 12 QTLs having LOD >3 and four with LOD score >5. Two QTLs of HNSMS had PVE >20% and four QTLs had PVE >30% in the corresponding environment. The most significant QTL for HNSMS was present on 2B chromosome. QHNSMS.pau‐2BS.3 was co‐located with the QTLs of HGY, HHGW, HGWMS, and HNGMS with the LOD score of 24.95 and phenotypic variance of 78.31%. There was no QTL found for this trait, which was present in the multiple environments.

The size of the QTL‐containing regions for QHNSMS had a range from 2.0 kb to 223.0 Mb with four regions of size less than 100 kb, three of size less than 1 Mb, and six of size less than 5 Mb (Table 4). The number of candidate genes in these regions varied from 1 to 1640 with an average of 185 genes per region. QHNSMS.pau‐2DL.2 had three candidate genes in a region of 67.1 kb, QHNSMS.pau‐3BS.1 had two candidate genes in a region of 64.3 kb, and QHNSMS.pau‐3BL.2 had four candidate genes in a region of 434.6 kb. QHNSMS.pau‐5DL.2 and QHNSMS.pau‐7BS.1 had one candidate gene in a region of 93.7 and 2.0 kb, respectively.

sec.title: QTLs for heat stress tolerance for spike length (HSL)
sec.p: Sixteen QTLs of HSL were detected through CIM on different chromosomes (Table 4; Figure S3). Positive allele for 10 QTLs was contributed by KSG0057 and for the remaining six QTLs by KSG1190. There were only specific QTLs for each environment, and there was no common QTL for any environment for HSL. Nine QTLs of HSL were detected for HS, two for SHS, and five for the difference between the two types of HS. There were eight QTLs of HSL specific for each year. However, when analyzed location‐wise, seven QTLs were specific for Ludhiana and nine for Hisar.

The range of LOD score for the QTLs of HSL varied from 2.51 to 5.43 with 10 QTLs having LOD >3 and one QTL having LOD >5. The phenotypic variance for the QTLs had a range from 8.40% to 60.44% with three QTLs having PVE >20% and only one QTL with PVE >30% in the respective environment. The most significant QTL, QHSL.pau.2BL, was co‐located with the QTL of HGY with an LOD score of 4.97 and PVE of 60.44%. There was no consistent QTL for HSL, which was present in the multiple environments.

Out of 16 regions containing QTLs for HSL, five regions had a size of less than 1 Mb and four had a size of less than 5 Mb with a range from 203.1 kb to 684.9 Mb (Table 4). The number of candidate genes in these regions ranged from 2 to 4869 with QTLs, QHSL.pau‐4AL, QHSL.pau‐5DS, and QHSL.pau‐1BS having 2, 3, and 5 candidate genes, respectively, in regions varying from 203.2 kb to 823.5 kb.

sec.title: QTLs for heat stress tolerance for plant height (HPH)
sec.p: Thirteen QTLs for HPH were located on seven chromosomes (Table 4; Figure S3). Three QTLs were present each on 2B and 2D chromosomes, two QTLs each on 3B and 6D chromosomes, and one QTL each on 1D, 5D, and 7B chromosomes. Of these 13 QTLs, eight were co‐located with the QTLs of other traits. The positive allele for seven QTLs was contributed by KSG0057, for five QTLs by KSG1190, and it was contributed by both the parents for the remaining one QTL. Three QTLs of HPH were found each for HS and SHS, and five QTLs were detected for the difference of the two types of HS. Six QTLs of HPH were specific for year 1 and another six were specific for year 2. Only one QTL was common during both the years. In locations, eight QTLs were specific for Ludhiana, four for Hisar, and one QTL was common for both the locations.

The range of LOD score for QTLs of HPH was between 2.59 and 5.87. Five QTLs of HPH had an LOD value of >3 and two QTLs had an LOD value of >5. With a range from 10.12% to 42.0%, two QTLs had PVE >20% and three had PVE >30% in the corresponding environment. The most significant QTL of HPH, QHPH.pau‐2BS.1, was co‐located with the QTL of HHGW with an LOD score of 3.02 and 42.0% PVE. Another QTL, QHPH.pau‐2DL.1, was found in multiple environments with the QTLs of other important traits having a significant LOD score ranging between 3.08 and 5.15 and PVE between 13.31% and 24.63%.

The size of QTL‐containing regions of HPH had a range from 13.7 kb to 257.0 Mb with two regions having size less than 100 kb and three with size less than 5 Mb (Table 4). The number of candidate genes in these regions had a range from 1 to 1201 with an average of 178 genes per region. There were two regions on 2D and 6D chromosomes with only one candidate gene and two regions on 2D and 3B chromosomes with less than 10 candidate genes.

sec.title: Common QTL regions of planting dates and HS tolerance
sec.p: In 66 QTL regions of planting dates and 100 QTL regions of HS tolerance, 38 were common QTL regions (Table 4; Figure S3). These regions were located on 1A, 1D, 2B, 2D, 3A, 3B, 5A, 5D, 6A, 6B, and 7B chromosomes. All the 12 regions on 2B chromosome identified for the QTLs of planting dates were common to the regions of HS tolerance. Of these 38 regions, 18 regions had the QTLs for same trait in the same environment. GY and HGW had 10 regions common between the two analyses. Only two regions, which was the least, were identified as common to each of SL and PH. Of 18, one region located on 2B chromosome had only one candidate gene. Another region on 2B chromosome had five candidate genes and one region on 3A chromosome had four candidate genes.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: As mentioned earlier, the female parent, KSG0057, is a selection out of a mega variety that was released in 1995 in India under the name PBW343 and its sister lines in other South‐East Asian countries. Just in few years after the release, it was cultivated on 7.28 million ha just in India alone. Screening for HS tolerance both under controlled as well as field conditions, we observed it to be significantly more susceptible than the male parent KSG1190, which was a selection out of an Australian variety, Sunstar, that is known for its drought tolerance and showed significant level of HS tolerance both under controlled as well as under field screening (Gill et al., unpublished data).

For the present study, two levels of HS during the flowering stage were given by delaying planting by 1 month for LS conditions and by 2 months for VLS conditions. Weather data from each of the experimental locations were obtained from the agrometeorological department of the respective universities (data not shown) and were used to evaluate the extent of HS during flowering for each of the planting conditions. As compared to normal planting, which was done during middle part of November, which enjoyed an ideal temperature of 14°C during flowering, LS planting was exposed to 5°C higher temperature (average 28.5°C) during flowering, and VLS was exposed to 32.5°C. We believe this is a reliable method of screening for flowering time HS tolerance, as this method, when compared to controlled condition heat screening, showed similar results for HS response (Gill, unpublished data).

As expected, both parental lines showed significant negative effects of LS and VLS conditions on all studied traits. On an average, KSG0057 showed 21.6% reduction in yield under LS and 52.8% under VLS as compared to 18.6% and 68.0%, respectively, for KSG1190. Similar difference was seen for the other traits. These results confirm that the two parents are significantly different in their response to HS given by manipulating planting time and thus are good parents to identify genes and QTLs controlling the studied traits. Maximum reduction was observed on GY and the least effect was observed on SL. On all locations, years, and traits, performance was less under LS in comparison to the NS and was the worst under VLS conditions. Considering that the plants were exposed to 5°C higher during flowering for LS and 11°C for VLS, these negative effects can be linked to HS during the flowering stage.

For GY, KSG1190 showed more reduction under VLS than KSG0057. This is not surprising because KSG0057 is adapted to the experimental locations, whereas KSG1190 is unadapted. That probably also explains the reduction in other traits also. As was observed under controlled conditions also (unpublished data), KSG1190 contributed significant positive alleles both under normal as well as under HS. This observation is also supported by the transgressive segregation observed for all traits (Figure 2; Table 1).

In general, the DH population showed normal distribution for all traits but there were differences in distribution among traits, locations, planting times, and even years. Five key differences in the distribution of the DH population are shown in Figure 2. The most dramatic difference was for GY under NS and VLS (Figure 2g,h). Under NS conditions, the distribution was significantly more distributed as compared to that under VLS conditions. The transgressive segregation, especially in the negative direction, was negligible under VLS as compared to that under normal NS conditions. This is probably because of the contribution of HS tolerance alleles by KSG1190. Similarly, the distributions were different between locations, years, and planting times for other traits also. We do not, however, have a reasonable explanation for the molecular or genetic basis of these differences.

Among traits, locations, years, and planting times, there were significant differences for the direction and the extent of transgressive segregation. For example, GWMS, for the Ludhiana location (L1, Figure 2i), showed transgressive segregation mainly in the negative direction, whereas at the Hisar location (L2, Figure 2j), the transgressive segregation was more balanced. Similarly, for GY under NS, transgressive segregation was significantly higher than that under VLS conditions, although the transgressive segregation for NS was mainly in the negative direction. We hypothesize that the extent and the direction of transgressive segregation can reveal the number and type of alleles differing between the two parents for the target traits. For example, the number of positive and negative alleles contributing to the trait differentiating between the two parents can be predicted from the extent and direction of the transgressive segregation. More transgressive segregation, as was seen for GY under NS conditions, suggested that more alleles with negative effect on the GY trait differ between the two parents. Less transgressive segregation for a trait under a particular condition suggests that there are less number of alleles differing between the two parents that control the trait under that condition, as was seen for GY under VLS conditions.

GY, HGW, GWMS, and NGMS are expected to be related traits and likely thus share underlying genes/QTLs. These traits showed significant positive correlation among them. Across locations and years, HGW and GWMS showed maximum correlation and both traits showed significant correlation with GY. Many of the QTLs for GY and these component traits were co‐localized, further indicating that either the same set of genes govern these traits or the underlying genes for these traits are tightly linked. Similar observations of correlated traits and yield component traits mapping in the same QTL regions were also made earlier (Bhusal et al., 2017; Kato et al., 2000).

The strong correlation of the GWMS with GY was surprising, as several other factors, such as tiller number and HGW, are expected to play a major role in determining GY. If this observation is validated in other populations, then GWMS can be used as a marker for GY.

The most surprising result was negative correlation between NSMS and GY, HGW, and GWMS. While the negative correlation between NSMS and HGW can be envisioned as more spikelets might compete for grain‐filling resources but the negative correlation with GWMS is very surprising, and we do not have a credible explanation for it. Another surprising correlation was between SL and PH. To our knowledge, this correlation has not been established earlier. If this turns out to be true, PH can be used as an indirect measure of HGW and GWMS as SL showed strong positive correlation with those traits. However, validation of these observations is needed in other populations before generalizing these relationships.

Overall, the GY was significantly higher during the 2017–2018 year as compared to 2016–2017 year (Table 1). If we compare the temperatures during flowering for the two seasons, it is evident that the maximum temperatures during the 2016–2017 season increased dramatically after March 18, the time when the flowering and grain filling is at its peak (Figure 1). During the same period during the 2017–2018 season, the weather stayed relatively mild suggesting that the yield difference between the 2 years can mainly be attributed to temperature during flowering confirming that HS played a major role in determining GY in this region.

Combined over the three planting dates, 155 QTLs were identified for the seven traits, which localized to 66 chromosomal regions. Of these, 25 were detected for normal season planting (NS) and 26 for LS. Under VLS condition, however, we detected 82 QTLs. These results validate that the two parents of the population have much less variable alleles for NS but have dramatically higher number of different alleles, reflected as significantly higher number of QTLs under VLS.

Very few QTLs were common among the three planting dates suggesting that the three planting dates are significantly different. There were five QTLs common between NS and LS and only three between NS and VLS highlighting the extent of difference in the environment during different planting dates. There were only two QTLs that were common among the three planting dates. Both of these QTLs were for GY. That is expected, as both lines are varieties and thus probably have stable and common alleles playing role in determining GY during all three planting dates. Between LS and VLS, however, there were 12 common QTLs highlighting that both late and very late planting expose plants to HS; thus, the alleles contributing to GY under HS are common during these two planting dates.

During HS, about an equal number of QTLs were identified during HS (40) and SHS (45). About an equal number of QTLs (44) were detected for the difference between the two types of HS clearly showing that the two types of HS are very different. This observation is also validated by the observation that very few (a total of six in all combinations) QTLs are common between the two types of HS.

Almost equal number of QTLs was observed for different planting dates (152) and the percent reduction (155), although the number of chromosomal regions containing the QTLs are significantly different. There were only 66 regions containing the 152 QTLs, whereas 100 regions contained the 155 QTLs observed. We do not have a reasonable explanation for this difference.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: This study was conducted to find the chromosomal regions associated with seven important traits, including GY, HGW, GWMS, NGMS, NSMS, SL, and PH under normal and heat‐stressed conditions. We have found 128 regions having 307 QTLs associated with different traits under study. These QTLs were detected for different planting dates, years, and locations and for the reduction percentages under HS conditions. The physical coordinates of these regions were appropriately marked and the number of genes underlying these regions was also determined. Sixteen regions were marked precisely to have only one candidate gene each. The QTLs found in this study can be used to design breeder‐friendly markers, which can further be utilized in marker‐assisted selection to pyramid these QTLs. Also, the identified candidate genes can be cloned and characterized.
